name: Cottonpet heritage walk.
description: Our fourth journey through the historic quarters of Kempe Gowda’s Pettah unfolds under a theme as timeless as it is universal—the search for Faith. Few places in Bengaluru bear witness to such layered expressions of belief, practice, and community as this old quarter, where stones, shrines, and stories alike speak of lives entwined with devotion.We begin in the western precincts of Pettah, which has one of the city’s most significant Sufi dargahs. For well over two centuries this shrine has stood not merely as a site of veneration but as a living symbol of spiritual devotion and communal harmony. Here, the life of the saint and the mystical traditions of Sufism unfold before us, reminding visitors of how such spaces once bridged communities across faiths, drawing pilgrims, merchants, and seekers into a shared spiritual geography.From the domain of sacred devotion we turn toward the realm of healing. In the narrow lanes nearby still operate age-old Ayurvedic massage centers, famed above all for their bone-setting traditions. Local memory recalls how the Maharajas of Mysore themselves entrusted these practitioners, as did the pahalwans of the akhadas—wrestling arenas that once gave Pettah its distinctive physical culture. In these practices of cure and discipline, body and faith intertwined, shaping a distinctly urban form of resilience and well-being.Our steps then carry us to venerable temples associated with saints whose teachings left a lasting imprint on the identity of this quarter. Within their carved stones and sanctums endures a layered continuity—of memory, worship, and the rhythm of everyday devotion. Time permitting, the trail may extend toward a garadi mane (wrestling house) or an old heritage lodge, each bearing traces of the social fabric of an earlier Bengaluru, when physical culture and communal gathering defined neighborhood life.The walk also includes a South Indian breakfast in heritage restaurant, where history, faith, and community meet in lived experience.This walk is guided by an architect whose professional eye discerns the city’s built heritage, and whose personal practice of Sufism and passion for food lend the journey both intimacy and delight. His explorations carry him to parts of Bengaluru often absent from tourist maps, offering participants not simply a tour, but an immersion into the city’s layered heart.

name: आज रंग है - Aaj Rang Hai
description: Aaj Rang HaiThere is a folk tale in Chishti circles about Amir Khusrau. He goes looking for a guru, finds Nizamuddin Auliya, and what comes out of him isn't a treatise but a song: aaj rang hai, today there is colour. Whether it happened quite like that, no one can say. But the song has been sung at the dargah in Delhi for about seven hundred years, and singers still turn to it when they want to name the moment when searching stops and something simply arrives.This evening's three sets come from three corners of the country, and from three different ways of living with that same question.Gurupriya Atreya and Vedanth Bharadwaj open with Kabir and the other Bhakti poets. Vedanth trained in Carnatic, Hindustani and Western classical music, and for years has sung the saint-poets, Bhakti and Sufi alike. Gurupriya sings with him. These verses were never meant to sit on a page. They were made to be sung among people, and that is how the two of them take them up.Santhi Priya follows with songs of the Bauls. For generations the Bauls of Bengal have been wanderers, singing about the moner manush, the person of the heart, the divine who lives in the body rather than in a temple or a mosque. Santhi Priya learned this music from her guru, Parvathy Baul, and is spoken of as the first woman from Kerala to sing it. A tradition this rooted in Bengal now has a voice from the other end of the country, which says something about how these songs have always moved: on foot, from teacher to student.After a short break, Mir Rajak and Group come to us from Pugal in Rajasthan. They are Mirasis, a hereditary community of musicians whose families have carried the Sufiyana kalam for centuries. In a single sitting they will go from Bulleh Shah and Khwaja Ghulam Farid to the bhajans of Kabir and Meera, without pausing to mark the change. For them there is no border to cross. The labels we bring, Sufi here and Bhakti there, are mostly our own.

name: Workshop - चलो हमारा देस - Chalo Hamara Des
description: Chalo hamara des, come to my country, is one of Kabir's recurring calls. The country he means is not on any map. It is his name for the place a seeker arrives at when the searching quiets down, and in the oral traditions of Malwa and elsewhere, singers have carried this invitation from village to village for centuries, mostly in the voices of people who never thought of themselves as performers.This workshop takes that call as its starting point. Over four and a half hours, we will learn and sing songs from Kabir, Meerabai and the Sufi kalam, and pay attention to what they are actually saying. Many of these songs begin with ordinary things: a pot, a thread, a well, a lamp, a road. From there they move, sometimes in a single line, towards what cannot be seen or named. We will follow that movement, starting with the familiar and letting the songs take us further in.The poets did not agree on one way of walking this road. Meera longs and waits. Kabir argues, mocks and asks awkward questions. The Sufis speak of remembrance, of surrender, of the beloved. We will spend time with each of these voices, and notice where they meet.You do not need to have sung before. These songs were made to be sung together, by people sitting on the ground, not by trained voices on a stage. What matters here is listening closely and joining in.

name: An Immersive Workshop - Jo Dooba So Paar
description: An immersive workshop with  Artists Vedanth Bharadwaj and Mir Rajak and team , its a musical journey into surrender through the songs of Meerabai, Kabir, and Sufi mystics.Jo Dooba So Paar is an invitation to surrender—to step beyond the instinct to hold on, control, and understand, and to discover what becomes possible when we allow ourselves to be carried by the song.The phrase carries a beautiful paradox. In ordinary life, we learn to keep ourselves afloat—to hold on to certainty, identity, control, and the familiar. But in the songs of mystics, surrender can become another kind of crossing. When the grip loosens, something deeper can reveal itself.Across the Bhakti and Sufi traditions, the language of drowning is not one of defeat. To drown is to let the separate self loosen its grip; to cross is to discover another shore. In this paradox lies the heart of the workshop: perhaps the way across is not through resistance, but through surrender.Through songs, poetry, collective singing and deep listening, we will explore longing, love, devotion, dissolution and the mysterious movement from 'I' towards something larger than oneself.Drawing from Kabir and Meerabai and Sufi saints, the workshop brings together diverse musical traditions that speak, in different voices, of the same inward movement.Sometimes, the shore is found only when we stop trying to stay afloat.Jo Dooba So Paar is an invitation to take that leap: to enter the song deeply enough that, for a moment, there is no need to know where we are going.Perhaps that is the mystery of the mystic's path—the one who dares to drown discovers that the other shore was never far away.No prior experience of singing is required. The emphasis is on listening, participation, voice and the shared experience of letting the song take us somewhere.

description: Grounds for Thought: October 2026 (Koramangala)A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesGrounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. name: Mycelium and Muse - Interactive Science Class
description: We often equate creativity with making art. Picasso was creative. Beethoven was creative. Van Gogh was creative.But what about the person who first picked up a piece of charcoal and scribbled on the wall of a cave, hoping the people in the next cave would get the message? Or the bowerbird who spends an entire season collecting blue bottle caps and flowers to decorate a little stage for a mate?And what about a fungus? This one is literally brainless, yet it sends out electrical signals that, when connected to a synthesizer, play out like music.So if creativity shows up in organisms without brains, it is far older than us, isn't it? That's the question we'll sit with over coffee: where creativity really begins on the tree of life, and what that means for those of us who have spent years saying "I'm just not the creative type."Along the way, you'll hear a mushroom play music, and you'll make something that is deliberately, wonderfully bad. You don't need any science background to join in.Just come, grab a coffee, and let's get some creativity brewing. Because, tell you what, I'm not sure a creative life is a happier one. But I'm pretty sure it's a far more meaningful one.About the Speaker:Bitasta Datta is a microbiologist by training, an educator by profession and a science storyteller by passion.For over 10 years, she has been turning science into stories for school learners and curious adults. She started at the National Digital Library of India, went on to co-found The Synapse, led curriculum and learning experience design at BYJU'S and Tutopiya, and tinkers with content at Khan Academy.

name: The gathering room - Edition II
description: The Gathering Room - IILast month, a room full of people who'd never met sat in a circle, and by the end of the afternoon, a simple dupatta had carried more than any of us expected it to. Some people spoke. Some didn't say a word. Almost everyone left a little lighter than they came in.We're doing it again.Divorce and separation don't end when the papers do. There's the decision itself. The legal process. And then everything after: the parenting schedule you're still figuring out, the money you're untangling, the boundaries you're learning to hold, often alone.Somewhere along the way, a story tends to settle in. That this is a failure. That it has to get ugly. That there's a "right" way to grieve, or a deadline for moving on.This session starts from a different place: a relationship changing shape isn't a verdict on who you are, and it doesn't have to look like a battle to be real.Whether you were with us last month or this is your first time, there's a seat for you. Mid-decision, past it, or still finding your way in.The FormatThis isn't a talk or a lecture.Expect some movement, a few structured activities in pairs or as a full group, and room throughout to simply notice where you are. No scripts, no performance. You don't need to prepare anything.What to ExpectArrivalCome in when you're ready. No forms, no forced small talk, no explanations owed.Opening CircleSeema, a Certified Psychodrama Practitioner who facilitates the session, will say hello and walk you through how the afternoon unfolds. If you'd like to share a word about why you're here, you can. If you'd rather listen, that's just as welcome.The Heart of the SessionThe main part of the afternoon: movement, a few activities in pairs or as a group, and quieter moments in between to check in with yourself. Nobody will ask you to talk if you don't want to. Nobody will ask you to perform.Coming Back TogetherBefore we close, we'll gather as a full group to sit with whatever came up. A reflection or a small gesture is welcome. So is silence.ClosingYou might leave with a bit more clarity. You might leave without saying a single word and still feel a little less alone. Both count.Each gathering builds on the last. Familiar faces make the room feel safer, and new ones remind everyone they're not the only ones going through this. Whether you were here in September or you're coming for the first time, there's a seat saved for you.

name: Bhima
description: BhimaSunday, 22nd November, 6.00 p.m. - 7.10 p.m.Language: EnglishAbout the PerformanceDrawing inspiration from Ashok Malhotra’s Child Man, MT Vasudevan Nair’s Randamoozham, and Jeanette Winterson’s Weight, this play explores the paradoxes and ironies in the life of the second Pandava, Bhima.Who is Bhima? What is his hunger? Who feeds it? What are the choices available to a hero? What is the fate of a strong man in contemporary times? These are some of the questions around which the key narrative of the play evolves. What is his relevance to contemporary life? Would his version of masculinity be acceptable in today’s world?If Bhima were to live today, who would he be — a loyal middle-management warrior who is the engine of the company but never its CEO? A family man who defines himself only in terms of roles — the breadwinner, the husband, the son — who will do anything for his family? Or does he exist as an individual beyond these roles? Trained under masters including Heisnam Kanhailal, Guru G. Venu, and at the Workcenter of Jerzy Grotowski and Thomas Richards, his practice integrates traditional Indian performance frameworks like Navarasa with contemporary physical theatre. His paper on his pedagogy of training contemporary actors in Navarasas has been selected for publication.As Artistic Director of Our Theatre Collective and Studio, Vivek leads experimental, research-driven performance initiatives. His original stage work includes directing the contemporary physical theatre piece The Thumb and acclaimed productions like IT IS YOU. He has acted in the feature film, Pada. Vivek has served as visiting faculty at Drama School Mumbai and Azim Premji University, and trained over 300 performers in India. He was named one of Forbes India’s 12 Boundary-Pushing Theatre Innovators.Sachin GurjaleSachin Gurjale is a theatre practitioner, drummer and sound designer and has been active in the Bengaluru cultural scene for over two decades. Sachin’s collaboration in the Bhima project dates back to 2014 when he travelled with Vivek to Iranjalakuda to study the role of the Mizhavu in a Koodiyattam performance under the guidance of Kalamandalam Rajeev. With this perspective, he designed a percussive score for Bhima that brought his own influence of the African djembe and other urban folk instruments.Anitha SanthanamAnitha Santhanam is a seasoned theatre and movement practitioner based in Bengaluru. Holding the embodied imagination as its core, her creative work spans performance, direction and teaching. She was part of the core faculty team at Drama School Mumbai (2022-2024), faculty of Integral Theatre on the FECAT program at SMART (2013-2022) and an artist-in-residence at the Srishti Manipal institute of Art, Design and Technology Bengaluru (2009-2013).Anitha is also a two-time awardee of the Charles Wallace India Trust scholarship through which she trained in actor-created theatre and the Lecoq pedagogy at LISPA London, under the mentorship of Thomas Pratkki.During her time in London, Anitha also trained with ARTIS education to facilitate integrated arts-in-education programs in schools and with JABADAO in developmental movement play for children. She is a trained Bharatanatyam performer and holds a diploma in Choreography from NIKC, Bengaluru.Photo Credits: Bharath TiwariAbout the FestivalPLAYINTERPLAY is a theatre festival with a difference. It celebrates 50 years of the Inlaks Shivdasani Foundation, bringing together its theatre awardees and scholars to show their work, share their experiences, skills and learnings, and converse on matters of common interest.PLAYINTERPLAY presents plays that are new to Bengaluru. What is different, however, is that it looks back as well as forward, featuring a work of theatre that has been specially revived for the festival and readings of plays that are still to become the finished article.PLAYINTERPLAY does more: it forges connections between its constituent parts — performances, workshops, conversations and experience sharing — emphasising the interplay between thought, learning and practice.See the plays! Apply for the workshops! Join the conversations! Soak in the magic of theatre.About the Artistic Director Anmol Vellani is the founder and former executive director of India Foundation for the Arts, the first independent philanthropic organisation in India devoted exclusively to supporting the arts. He is also the co-founder of Toto Funds the Arts, which nurtures, encourages and rewards new voices and emerging talent in the arts.Anmol did not, however, aspire to become a professional in the field of philanthropy. His early fascination was with the arts, especially theatre and music, and also philosophy, which he studied at the Universities of Poona, Oxford and Cambridge. He taught ethics, logic and the history of philosophy at Elphinstone College, Mumbai, in the 1970s.His writing and talks — on arts entrepreneurship, the creative economy, cultural policy, the role of grant-making foundations, culture and development, arts collaboration and the performing arts, for example — have reflected on the insights he has gleaned from his long engagement with the arts and philanthropy.Anmol has been associated with nearly 50 plays as a director, designer or actor. He has directed theatre productions in different languages and cities. His last two plays — Innocence (2024) and Apne Ghar Jaisa (2022) — have been lauded for their sharp and critical look at contemporary social and political realities in India.

name: The Death of Galileo
description: The Death of GalileoWednesday, 25th November, 7.30 p.m. - 8.50 p.m.Language: HindiAbout the PerformanceThis play is an adaptation of Bertolt Brecht’s Life of Galileo. Using a non-linear theatrical structure, it connects Galileo’s struggle to contemporary realities.The play unfolds at night inside a museum, where a group arrives to demolish its collection of cultural and collective living memories and objects. Among the artefacts, they discover a telescope, which becomes the point of departure for the story of Galileo — his discoveries, struggles, confinement and unceasing search for truth. As the night progresses, Galileo’s time and the present time begin to unfold simultaneously, revealing parallels between social realities in two different historical moments.The members of the demolition group are themselves caught between disillusionment, violence and self-deception. Their encounter with the museum and with Galileo stirs their conscience, and while one group remains adamant, the other begins to question its reasons for wanting to destroy the museum. An internal conflict begins, between the path they’ve chosen, to raze the museum for their pride, and the path their conscience wants to guide them towards. description: Kadambari: Tracing Fragments of a Shattered MuseFriday, 27th November, 7.30 p.m - 9.00 p.m.Language: Hindi, BengaliAbout the PerformanceKadambari is a lyrical theatrical journey into the silenced life of Kadambari Devi, Rabindranath Tagore’s critic, muse, companion, and sister-in-law, married into the Tagore household at nine and gone by 25, when the poet himself was only 23. Rather than reducing her to a footnote in his biography, the play seeks to restore her voice, weaving memory, fiction and imagination. It traces fragments of her existence beyond whispers of scandal and tragedy, asking how history chooses to remember or erase the women who stand behind celebrated men.Set during her final hours, the play imagines Death arriving to claim her. description: Full FrontalSaturday, 28th November, 7.30 p.m. - 8.30 p.m.Language: EnglishAbout the PerformanceEnter Vinod. He is a man’s man. He is an actor. He is a lover. He is a delight. As memory, desire, myth, cinema and conditioning collide, the audition room becomes a space where masculinity is continuously performed, interrogated and disrupted.Is a feminist man simply another role to master? name: Physical Theatre: Its Possibilities and Limits
description: Physical Theatre: Its Possibilities and LimitsA Conversation with Tushar Pandey, Ashwath Bhatt and Vivek Vijayakumaran, moderated by Anmol Vellani Sunday, 22nd November, 7.30 p.m. - 9.00 p.m.About the ConversationPhysical theatre communicates primarily, though not solely, through the language of gestures, facial expressions and movement. The exception is mime, which is non-verbal by definition.In this session, three theatre artists will speak about what attracted them to physical theatre and describe the nature of their involvement in the teaching and practice of this stylised form of performance. As their work as directors and actors has also extended beyond physical theatre, they will reflect on the reasons for their divergent artistic choices.Physical theatre has many strengths. Most notably, it can overcome language barriers, express what words cannot, connect with audiences at a visceral level, harness the ideas and creativity of the whole group, and rely on minimalist scenography. But equally, it is constrained by the very characteristics that set it apart from other theatre styles. This session will conclude with a discussion on the limits of physical theatre and the creative strategies that can prevent style from overshadowing substance.About the ParticipantsAshwath BhattAshwath Bhatt is a Mumbai-based screen and stage artist, who has worked with acclaimed filmmakers and reputed theatre companies both in India and abroad. He has acted under the direction of various Indian and international theatre luminaries, and conducted workshops on various aspects of acting worldwide. He serves on the selection panel of LAMDA in India as well as for the Inlaks Theatre Awards, of which he is the co-creator. He teaches at various prestigious institutions in India and overseas. He is widely known for his work on the ‘Red Nose Clowning’ in India. In 2007, he established a nonprofit trust called the Theatre Garage Project. His work is guided by the idea of finding something in nothing. He recently directed the play Paladin based on the best-selling book When Breath Becomes Air by Dr. Paul Kalanithi.Tushar PandeyTushar Pandey is an actor, director and theatre educator with over two decades of experience in performance, teaching and devised theatre. He is a graduate of the National School of Drama, India, and has trained in physical theatre and Lecoq pedagogy at the London International School of Performing Arts (LISPA), London.His work has involved acting, directing, devising and teaching across theatre and film, with a particular interest in movement, physicality and the relationship between text and performance. He has worked on projects in India and internationally, including in England, Scotland, Greece, Dubai and China.Tushar serves on the Board of the Drama Schools Foundation Mumbai and has been a guest faculty at the National School of Drama, Delhi and Sikkim. His screen work includes Chhichhore, Pink, Hum Chaar, Lost and Aashram.Vivek VijayakumaranVivek Vijayakumaran is a Bengaluru-based theatre director, actor, and pedagogue with over 15 years of experience in performance, embodied research, and actor training. Venu, and at the Workcenter of Jerzy Grotowski and Thomas Richards, his practice integrates traditional Indian performance frameworks like Navarasa with contemporary physical theatre. We will learn from them if writing science fiction for the theatre poses unique challenges. They will reference their own plays to demonstrate that science fiction is not a form of free-floating fantasy; it can, for instance, address moral dilemmas and ask searching questions about the political tendencies of our times.Script Reading:Juno 77By Abhishek MajumdarIn Juno 77, a woman disappears during a space mission. Her partner’s search takes him far beyond Earth, where time unsettles everything they believed they knew about love, duty, and family. When their paths cross again, each has lived differently and in different references of time since the separation. How should they now understand their obligations to one another?Against this story, Juno 77 asks questions at the heart of moral philosophy. Does an intention matter more than its consequences? Can someone be held to a promise in circumstances no one could have imagined? What does it mean to forgive a person whose absence has shaped your entire life?The play also considers how religion helps us live with such questions. Faith offers ways to think about time, sacrifice, suffering and the possibility of reunion. Yet those ideas can mean different things to people who have endured the same loss differently. Bringing space science into conversation with religious thought, Juno 77 asks how we make moral choices when our shared understanding of a life has come apart. name: How Not to Build a Theatre Institution
description: How Not to Build a Theatre InstitutionA Conversation with Abhishek Mudgal, Sanyukta Saha and Abhishek Majumdar, moderated by Priyanka Varma Friday, 27th November, 5.00 p.m. - 6.30 p.m.About the ConversationArtists establish and lead theatre institutions (which include long-standing initiatives) for different reasons — to practice, teach, present, advocate or support the art form, for instance.But such undertakings, especially if they function independently of secure government or corporate largesse, can falter or fail. The poverty of infrastructure and support for the theatre are among the external factors that are adduced for the precariousness of artist-led institutions. Internal factors are rarely cited. What if the institution is over-reliant on personal equations and goodwill for its sustenance? Or if its ownership is narrowly concentrated in one or two charismatic personalities? Or if it is too obsessed with legacy concerns to avert obsolescence in a swiftly changing environment?This session will investigate what might lie inside any theatre institution that could threaten its stability and hamper its growth. Reflecting on their personal experience of founding and running institutions, three theatre artists will tell us about what worked or did not work about the choices they made. Were discontents allowed to simmer, tensions swept under the carpet or challenges left unaddressed? In hindsight, do they regret any missteps or wish they had done some things differently?About the Participants Sanyukta SahaSanyukta Saha is a theatre pedagogue, facilitator and community arts leader, and the Founder and Executive Director of Aagaaz Theatre Trust, a community-rooted arts organisation in New Delhi. name: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre
description: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre A Conversation with Sharanya Ramprakash, Laya N Kumar and Parshathy J Nath, moderated by Lakshmana KP Saturday, 28th November, 4.30 p.m. - 6.00 p.m.About the ConversationThe traditions with which contemporary urban Indian theatre artists can engage are immense, embracing mythologies, folk tales and performances, art and craft objects and practices, festivals and rituals, cuisine, inherited knowledge and skills, and much else besides. At the same time, the distinction between the traditional and the modern is not clearcut. Modern theatre in India has a history that stretches back for over two centuries — long enough to develop its own traditions. Dance forms now regarded as ‘classical’ acquired modern practices of teaching, performance and patronage in the last century.The theatre artists in this session will speak about their idea of tradition and how they have interacted with it in the plays they have written, directed or performed. They will also be invited to discuss ethical and political questions that come to the fore when tradition is brought into contemporary theatre work. Has their work been sensitive to the claim that borrowing from inherited forms of expression can constitute a form of cultural theft or disrespects localised and context-specific creation of value and meaning? How would they negotiate with traditions that have been invented in response to market demands or political pressures? Has their work reconciled with, or has it offered a critical perspective on the feudalism, casteism and gender discrimination embedded in many traditional performances and stories?About the ParticipantsSharanya Ramprakash Sharanya Ramprakash is a Bengaluru-based theatre-maker. She places her work at the intersection of gender, tradition and language. She writes, acts, directs and collaborates with a range of forms, communities and theatre-makers across local, national and international locations. Her work is research-based, collaborative and exploratory. She is a member of the Lincoln Centre Director’s Lab, New York. She is also a recipient of the Shankar Nag Theatre Award 2022.Parshathy J NathParshathy J Nath is a theatre artist based in Bengaluru. Over the last ten years, she has worked with some of the best-known theatre directors in south India, including Prasanna Ramaswamy, Rajiv Krishnan, Vinay Kumar, Nimmy Raphel, Sharanya Ramprakash, Aruna Ganesh Ram, Koumarane Valavane and Sanjeeva Suvarna. She has trained at Adishakti Laboratory for Theatre Art Research, Ninasam and Natanakairali. In 2025, she received a production grant from the India Foundation for Arts, with which she created a solo performance piece called Shoorpanakha: A Search. This production has travelled to different cities and has been performed at The School of Drama and Fine Arts, Kerala, Kerala Sangeetha Nataka Akademi, Ranga Shankara, and BLR Hubba 2025.Laya N KumarLaya Kumar has trained with groups like Indian Ensemble, IAPAR and Bhasha Centre, and with award-winning theatre-makers, including Mahesh Dattani and Gurleen Judge. She has worked as a producer on Naatak Express, a fundraiser festival that brings together over 100 artists to make short plays in 24 hours. description: DramatherapyExperience Sharing by Vardhan DeshpandeSaturday, 28th November, 3.00 p.m. - 4.00 p.m.About the SessionIn this session, Vardhan Deshpande reflects on his journey with Dramatherapy and its possibilities as a practice of healing, expression and transformation.Over the past two-and-a-half years, he has been working with children at risk through Dramatherapy sessions, alongside six months of work with specially-abled children. This journey has involved much more than conducting sessions — it has been a continuous process of observing, designing, planning, facilitating, implementing, documenting and reflecting. Each group and every individual encounter has shaped his understanding of how theatre, play, imagination, embodiment, storytelling and creative expression can create spaces for children to explore themselves, connect with others and experience agency.The session will share key experiences from this practice: the challenges encountered, the learning that emerged, the questions that continue to remain, and the ways in which reflection has influenced subsequent interventions. It will also look towards the future — considering how Dramatherapy and Applied Theatre can evolve in working with children and communities, and the ethical, creative and contextual sensitivities that such practice demands.About the SpeakerVardhan DeshpandeVardhan Deshpande works as a theatre facilitator in schools and colleges. name: Lecture-Demonstration on the Folk Theatre of Bayalata
description: Experience Sharing by Dr Sahana PinjarLecture-Demonstration on the Folk Theatre of BayalataMonday, 23rd November, 7.00 p.m. - 8.00 p.m.About the SessionDr. Sahana Pinjar will be presenting a live demonstration of the traditional Kannada folk-theatre form of Bayalata through the performance of Girija Kalyana, depicting the divine marriage of Girija (Parvati) and Lord Shiva. The demonstration will showcase the storytelling, acting, dialogue, traditional movements, music, costumes, and theatrical conventions of Bayalata, bringing the story to life for a contemporary audience. The story, written by Dr. Basavaraja Malshati, portrays Girija’s deep devotion and determination to attain Lord Shiva, her penance, and the eventual divine wedding. Through lively characters, expressive acting, traditional music and the energetic style of Bayalata, the narrative unfolds as both a sacred tale and a vibrant theatrical experience. The performance celebrates themes of devotion, love, perseverance and the union of divine energies, while preserving the distinctive visual and performative elements of Karnataka’s folk theatre tradition.CastGirija and Rathi: Dr. Sahana PinjarShiva: Syed Sadiq SManmatha: Nehar AhamadaSutradhara: Anklesh HSarathi: K NagarajMusicTabla: GadhlingappaHarmonium: EraswamiAbout the ArtistsDr. Sahana PinjarA dedicated theatre practitioner, researcher, and CCRT Senior Fellow, Sahana‘s creative practice spans grassroots cultural documentation, indigenous folk traditions, and community-engaged arts. Currently a Syndicate member of Karnataka Folklore University and a former member of Ranga Samaja, she has trained at Ninasam and the National School of Drama, and has a Ph.D. from Bangalore University.She has participated in workshops with the American Bread and Puppet Theatre, and the Swedish Centre of the ITI and SIDA where she learned to apply theatre methodologies to formal education. She also completed an acting workshop based on the Grotowski system by experts from Teatr Zar, Poland, along with a workshop on Lighting and Stage Management by experts from the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, England.Having worked with renowned directors, her practice bridges rigorous academic research and social advocacy. She leads youth and children's theatre through Hosapete's 'Bahutva Kala Tanda' and conducts inclusive workshops for marginalised youth. She has been recognised as one of the Deccan Herald Changemakers in 2025, and has received the Ranga Ratna Award 2026, an India Foundation for the Arts’ Kali Kalisu Project Grant 2016 and an HRD Scholarship. Her work serves as a vital conduit for cultural preservation, empowering grassroots traditions and fostering community dialogue.Syed Sadiq SSyed Sadiq S is an actor, director and theatre educator with over 15 years of sustained engagement with theatre in Karnataka. For him, theatre is not merely a performing art but a powerful medium for learning, self-expression, dialogue, connecting with people and communities, and understanding the complexities of human experience.He holds a Master’s degree in Cooperative Management from the University of Mysore and a Master’s degree in Theatre from Karnataka State Dr. Gangubai Hangal Music and Performing Arts University, Mysuru. In 2013–14, he underwent intensive professional theatre training at the Ninasam Theatre Institute, Heggodu.He is based in Hosapete, where he founded Bahutva, an arts organisation committed to introducing theatre to children and young people. name: The World in the Body: Observe. Absorb. Create.
description: The World in the Body: Observe. Absorb. Create. A Workshop by Tushar Pandey.Sunday, 22nd November, 10.00 a.m. - 3.00 p.m.Points to NoteYour place in the workshop will be confirmed only after payment and final selection. If you are not selected, the fee will be refunded.If you are selected and attend the entire workshop, the fee will be refunded.If you are selected and there is a no-show, or if you attend only part of the workshop, there will be no refund.About the WorkshopThis workshop explores the immense possibilities of the performer’s body and mind, and the relationship between the body, space and the world around us. Through observation, physical exploration and play, participants will draw from the rhythms, movements, textures and dynamics of nature, objects, people and spaces, allowing these external influences to become internal impulses and material for performance. The work moves between the external and the internal: what moves us, what creates an impulse, and how physical sensation can lead to emotion, sound, words and eventually images.Imagination and physicality become tools for exploring different theatrical languages, from realistic text and dramatic composition to epic storytelling and grotesque or comic worlds.About the FacilitatorTushar PandeyTushar Pandey is an actor, director and theatre educator with over two decades of experience in performance, teaching and devised theatre. He is a graduate of the National School of Drama, India, and has trained in physical theatre and Lecoq pedagogy at the London International School of Performing Arts (LISPA), London. His work has involved acting, directing, devising and teaching across theatre and film, with a particular interest in movement, physicality and the relationship between text and performance. He has worked on projects in India and internationally, including in England, Scotland, Greece, Dubai and China. Tushar serves on the Board of the Drama Schools Foundation Mumbai and has been a guest faculty at the National School of Drama, Delhi and Sikkim. His screen work includes Chhichhore, Pink, Hum Chaar, Lost and Aashram.Applicants to NoteApplicants are required to fill in the form linked below to give us an understanding of their experience, interests and more.Workshop Application Form - The World in the BodyEligibility Age: Preferably 18 years and above. No upper age limit, provided participants are comfortable with movement-based work.Experience: Open to actors, theatre-makers, performers, dancers and students of performance. name: Mycelium & Muse: A Science Storytelling Workshop
description: About the Workshop:We often equate creativity with making art. Picasso was creative. Beethoven was creative. Van Gogh was creative.But what about the person who first picked up a piece of charcoal and scribbled on the wall of a cave, hoping the people in the next cave would get the message? Or the bowerbird who spends an entire season collecting blue bottle caps and flowers to decorate a little stage for a mate?And what about a fungus? This one is literally brainless, yet it sends out electrical signals that, when connected to a synthesiser, play out like music.So if creativity shows up in organisms without brains, it is far older than us, isn't it?That's the question we'll sit with: Where does creativity really begin on the tree of life, and what does that mean for all of us who have spent years saying "I'm just not the creative type". Along the way, you'll hear a mushroom playing music, make an idea card that is deliberately, wonderfully bad, write a letter to your future self, and discover a new answer to the question “Am I creative?”You don't need any science background to join in. Just come in, and let's get some creativity brewing.Because, tell you what, we are not sure if a creative life is a happier one. But what we can absolutely guarantee is that it's a far more meaningful one.About the facilitator:Bitasta Datta is a microbiologist by training, an educator by profession and a science storyteller by passion.For over 10 years, she has been turning science into stories for school learners and curious adults. She started at the National Digital Library of India, went on to co-found The Synapse, led curriculum and learning experience design at BYJU'S and Tutopiya, and now leads the efforts at Khan Academy India to narrate science in a way that sticks.She believes science and art are two lenses on the same world, and that if you look through both long enough, you arrive at the same philosophy. So that's what she does. She dissects science to find the art in it, dissects art to find the science in it, and narrates her findings as stories.Outside work, she paints, bakes, and travels, and writes about the places where science, art and philosophy run into each other. Mycelium & Muse began as one of those pieces.
